en: Volume Four, Part Two.
Composed by Li Tongxuan of the Great Tang at Beiping.
The Tenth Stage, the Cloud of Dharma (Dharmameghā-bhūmi), takes the Perfection of Wisdom as its primary focus, with the remaining nine perfections serving as its companions. This—
In the city of Kapilavastu, there was a woman of the Śākya clan named Gopā who, by clarifying the practices of the ten stages (*daśabhūmi*), did not depart from her original place.

She remained in the same location as the first stage to signify that the essence of bodhi has no sequence of before or after and remains unchanged from beginning to end; therefore, it is said that in the city of Kapilavastu there was a woman of the Śākya clan.
Gopā was, in fact, the wife of the Tathāgata when he was a prince in a former life.

More than a hundred kalpas ago, as numerous as the atoms in a buddha-field, there was a king named Jñānagiri; the king had a crown prince named Suprabha, and a householder’s daughter named Vimalasūryā.
The Crown Prince Śubhaprabha left the household life to become a bhikṣu and resided in the Forest of Pure Virtue (Vimalaguṇa).

When he entered the city to beg for alms, the maiden Vimaladattā saw the bhikṣu Śubhaprabha; she immediately conceived a defiled attachment toward him, so she untied the jeweled necklaces from her body, placed them along with pearls into his alms bowl, and instantly gave rise to the bodhicitta.
For two hundred and fifty kalpas, he will no longer fall into the three evil realms, but will always be born in superior and blissful places, constantly seeing the bhikṣu Śubhaprabha.
After these two hundred and fifty kalpas, he will be born into the family of Suprabuddha, arising through transformation within a lotus flower.
She saw that King Dhanapati had a crown prince named Tejas; she took him as her husband.
Thereafter, she constantly made offerings to the Buddhas together with the prince, until she heard the Dharma and attained the Way.
Even until the time when the Tathāgata was a crown prince, she remained his wife.
This was due to the causal conditions of her original vow in the past, whereby she constantly served as his consort.
As the ancient masters have said:
"When the Tathāgata was a crown prince, he had three consorts:
the first was Yaśodharā, the mother of Rāhula, who became a bhikṣuṇī;
the second was named Gopā, who became a spiritual friend (kalyāṇamitra) on the ten stages (daśabhūmi) of Sudhana."
"The three named Manuṣas have not yet been clearly identified as to their location.
Now, the divine wisdom of the Tathāgata is identical in nature to empty space; no material form can be its equal.
As for the essence of this wisdom, no sentient conceptualization can trace its mark.

Yet, by means of this wondrous spirit that lacks form or substance, it universally responds throughout the ten directions according to the faculties [of beings]: for those of superior faculties, a lotus flower appears;
for those of middling or inferior capacities, it is born from a mother’s womb.

It is solely because of the power of the benevolence of his original vow that he manifests forms according to the needs of beings throughout the worlds of the ten directions; how could he possibly remain in the world while maintaining a wife and children?

It is solely for the sake of transforming the ordinary and guiding the mundane that he manifests birth among humans; though the eighty-four thousand deluded minds follow him in his conduct, he transforms his wife and illusory children, and transforms illusory sentient beings, manifesting as one dwelling within entanglements, yet able to renounce what is difficult to renounce.
Regarding the seeds of the three vehicles, one discards all ornaments;

yet, corresponding to the gateway of the fruit of Buddhahood in the One Vehicle, one is endowed with a flower crown, necklaces, the ninety-seven marks of a Great Man, and marks as numerous as the atoms within ten Flower Treasury worlds.
Now, by means of the maiden Gopā, the wisdom-realm of the One Vehicle is symbolized; there is no separate seeking of transcendence.

With fundamental wisdom, all things universally seal the mundane world, such that the myriad objects are entirely true. It is not said that there is a separate pure land elsewhere; rather, Gopā is used to represent the same true nature, wherein there is no dharma of grasping or rejecting. Thus, she serves as a symbol for the Dharma, clarifying that the ten stages of the path are fulfilled and that the joy of the Dharma serves as one’s consort.
All realms of experience are, in their entirety, the joy of the Dharma.
Therefore, the *Lotus Sūtra* unifies the three vehicles into the One Vehicle, stating that "the characteristics of the world are eternally abiding; this is the Dharma abiding in its own place."
He regards the entire world as liberation, without any further distinction between what is to be rejoiced in and what is to be loathed.

Furthermore, this assembly of the sutra consists only of five hundred upāsakas, five hundred upāsikās, five hundred boys, five hundred girls, and ten thousand nāgas; it is a gathering solely of worldly laypeople, with no bhikṣus from the supramundane community present.
The Tathāgata is the practice of the perfection of merit, wisdom, and great compassion; he is a form that never tires of appearing in the world.
Now, by means of the girl Gopā, he symbolizes the joy of the ten stages (daśabhūmi), wherein there is no grasping or rejecting of phenomena.
Therefore, the *Vimalakīrtinirdeśa Sūtra* states: "Dharma-joy is taken as a wife; compassion is taken as a daughter.

As for Sudhana’s arrival at the Universal Radiance Dharma Hall where Bodhisattvas assemble throughout the entire dharma-realm, it is because he has reached the fulfillment of the wisdom of the tenfold turning of the wheel of Dharma.
This is the first assembly at the site of enlightenment, wherein one accords with the Wisdom of Universal Radiance; it is also the second assembly in the Hall of Universal Light.

From the second assembly onward, one personally gives rise to faith and advances in practice until reaching the ten stages (*daśabhūmi*). Having fulfilled the path of wisdom by one's own means, one becomes identical to the wisdom of the Dharma-wheel of all Buddhas. Because this constitutes the culmination, it is called the Bodhisattva Assembly in the Hall of Universal Radiance that Universally Manifests the Dharma-realm.

Among them was the presiding deity of the palace named Aśoka-guṇa, who, together with ten thousand palace-guarding deities, came to welcome Sudhana and praised the roots of goodness cultivated by him as the cause for entering the ten stages.
The vision of the maiden Gopā is the fruit of the tenth stage (*daśabhūmi*).
The ten thousand palace-guarding deities are the protectors of the conduct of wisdom and compassion of the tenth stage.

Although the maiden Gopā has made offerings to countless Buddhas and served Vairocana for eons past, having herself attained the rank of the tenth stage, she still says that she does not yet fully understand the bodhisattva’s body and bodily karma, nor does she know his mental wisdom.

Regarding the path traversed throughout all kalpas: by means of the gateway of Samantabhadra’s practices prior to entering the stage of Equal Enlightenment, one proceeds until the ten stages (bhūmis) are perfected. At that point, one must completely abandon the afflictions of the path of seeing (*darśana-mārga*), the higher afflictions of dhyāna-samādhi, and the higher afflictions regarding the pure bliss of nirvāṇa. Constantly entering the world, one manifests a form-body (*rūpa-kāya*) before all sentient beings to teach, transform, benefit, and bring them joy; this is the eternal path, wherein there is no further mind of longing or striving for supramundane samādhi, nirvāṇa, liberation, or even their residual habits (*vāsanā*).
Thus, as described in the sutras, when the practices of the ten stages were fulfilled, he sought Samantabhadra through immeasurable samādhis but was utterly unable to see him.
The Buddha exhorted him to seek and find him through mental visualization; only then did he see Samantabhadra appearing and disappearing before all the Buddhas of the ten directions.
By establishing this model through Gopā, it serves to perfect future learners, enabling them to understand the rules of conduct so that they may practice without confusion.
From the passage "From me, he has only attained this liberation of the ocean-like samādhi of the Bodhisattva" onwards, this constitutes the promotion of his virtues.
The above concludes the section on the spiritual friends (*kalyāṇamitra*) of the ten stages (*bhūmi*).
Regarding the conduct of Samantabhadra at the stage of Equal Enlightenment (*samyak-saṃbodhi*) of the eleventh stage, it is as follows.

From the initial mind of the first dwelling (*vihāra*) up to the fulfillment of the tenth dwelling, the daughter of King Siṃhadhvaja attained one portion of mundane and supramundane wisdom and perfected her compassion.

From the beginning of the ten stages of practice (*daśabhūmi*) until their completion, those who have left the household life and are non-Buddhist practitioners are called "universal practitioners" (*paryāpanna*); they attain a portion of the practice of conformity and achieve an untainted liberation through the non-destruction of their renunciation.

From the first of the ten dedications until their completion, one perceives the deities of heaven and earth, who possess mastery in nourishing all through the practice of wisdom and compassion regarding the cycle of birth and death within the world.
From the first stage of the ten stages to their fulfillment, they beheld the lady Gopā within the Universal Manifestation Hall of the Dharma-realm at the assembly of bodhisattvas;

as well as the spirit Aśokaśrī and ten thousand palace-guarding spirits, who, through the paths of the ten stages, have equalized their wisdom with that of all Buddhas and possess mastery in wisdom and compassion regarding the turning of the wheel of Dharma.

From the stage of Universal Worthy Bodhisattva’s practice at the eleventh ground of Equal Enlightenment, beginning with Māyādevī up to the fulfillment of the eleventh ground, one beholds the youth Guṇākara and the maiden Guṇavatī; by constantly proceeding through the six realms of birth and death in the ten directions and entering the gate of illusory abiding, the merit of the stage of Equal Enlightenment is brought to completion.

Mañjuśrī, Maitreya Tathāgata, and Samantabhadra Bodhisattva—these three persons collectively embody the five stages as well as the essence and function of the Dharma-realm gate within the stage of the ten faiths, which is the wondrous practice of the single principle and wisdom.
From the initial generation of the bodhicitta until the fulfillment of the five stages, one never departs from these three dharmas.
Mañjuśrī is the sublime wisdom of liberation through the three emptinesses; it is the subtle discernment of the principles of the correct and the false.

Maitreya Tathāgata entrusts himself to this same teaching because he attains the fruit of Buddhahood within a single lifetime; thus, it is the fundamental wisdom of universal radiance (*samantaprabhā-jñāna*).
Samantabhadra is the gate of practice for benefiting sentient beings through the wisdom of differentiation within that fundamental wisdom of universal radiance.
The three dharmas are the gateway to the unity of essence and function; thus, one is able to attain mastery over all phenomena.
These three dharmas constitute the doctrinal essence (*śarīra*) of this entire section of the sutra, and for this reason, it is called the Perfect Teaching of the One Vehicle (*ekayāna*).
From the cultivation of the ten levels of faith until the completion of the five stages, one always takes Mañjuśrī as the foremost guide for discernment and Samantabhadra as one’s companion.
Upon reaching the gateway to the fruition of entering the Dharma-realm, Samantabhadra is the leader and Mañjuśrī is the companion.

Fundamental wisdom (mūla-jñāna) constantly serves as the undefiled essence of these two dharmas. If fundamental wisdom has not yet been clarified, it is manifested through the contemplative observation of wondrous wisdom (prajñā);
if fundamental wisdom is clarified, then wondrous wisdom is the sublime messenger of fundamental wisdom.

Samantabhadra is the essence of the myriad practices within fundamental wisdom; in total, this single dharma is divided into three aspects: principle, wisdom, and great compassion, which constitute the essence and function.

If one does not thus distinguish between their union and separation, the practitioner will not understand that wisdom, compassion, essence, and function possess the mastery of penetration and obstruction.
Mañjuśrī emerged from the Sudharmā Pavilion and traveled south to transform and benefit the human realm and awaken the ignorant; therefore, he is named Mañjuśrī Kumārabhūta.

The Bodhisattva establishes their name based on the causal practice of the wisdom that perceives the Path for the sake of transforming the ignorant; therefore, before seeing the Path, they attain fundamental wisdom through discerning insight.
After seeing the Path, this insight serves as the messenger of the Buddha.
This can be understood by observing the essential meaning.
In all cases, the essence and function of wisdom and principle interpenetrate one another.
At the initial stage of the Equal Enlightenment (samyak-saṃbodhi) position, the perfection of giving (dāna-pāramitā) serves as the primary factor, while the other nine serve as its companions.

Regarding the Buddha’s mother, Māyā, who exists within this world: she is able, from this station, to dwell amidst the realm of birth and death while universally encompassing all worldly spheres with a heart of great compassion. Without distinguishing between internal and external, or east, west, south, and north, it is said simply that she dwells within this world.

Regarding the "Mother of Buddhas": the Tathāgata takes great compassion as the essence of motherhood, for she is able to give rise to great wisdom and transform sentient beings; thus, in reality, she is not born in the manner of worldly parents.
Out of great kindness and great compassion, not departing from their initial resolve, they transform sentient beings through the power of their original vows;

thus, it is appropriate that they be seen in such ways. By means of their own wisdom, they conjure themselves as parents or as wives and children, or manifest through lotus-birth; they adopt various modes of birth to accord with the conduct of sentient beings, appearing in whatever form is suitable for transformation. All of these are the realm of the Tathāgata’s single wisdom, manifested through illusory means as circumstances require. How, then, could there be the marks of being born from parents, entering the womb, emerging from the womb, or the phenomena of going and staying?

One should aspire to their self-wisdom, which, by its very essence, is wondrous and subtle: it is without color or form, without trace or defilement, and is pure in its own nature. Furthermore, through the power of great compassion in accordance with original vows, it possesses the merits of the two retributions—the environment and its inhabitants—and is adorned with blessings and wisdom. Like a reflection in light, it cannot be grasped; its concealment and manifestation are sovereign, like the pavilion of Maitreya or the Flower Treasury World.
They dwell together with all sentient beings, each without mutual obstruction; the body is the primary retribution (*vipāka*), while the land is the secondary retribution (*niśraya-vipāka*).
Furthermore, these two types of retribution—the primary and the secondary—interpenetrate one another, like the jewel-net of Śakra, where light and shadow intermingle in infinite layers.
Thus, Lady Māyā and the Tathāgata’s retinue are all produced through the illusory transformation of the single fundamental wisdom.
Because she receives the ignorant, she acts as a mother through great compassion, manifesting the Buddha through illusion.

Just as at the end of the tenth stage (*daśabhūmi*), compassion arises from wisdom—as exemplified by the daughter of King Siṃhadhvaja named Maitrīcaryā—so too at this stage of perfect enlightenment (*samyaksaṃbodhi*), wisdom arises from compassion; thus, it is through the mother that the Buddha is born.
The stages of advancement are likewise so.
Sudhana praised the body of Lady Māyā, saying: "It transcends the six sense bases and is free from all attachments; it is the unimpeded path of wisdom, endowed with the pure Dharma-body."

One manifests transformation bodies through karma that is like an illusion, manifests the world through wisdom that is like an illusion, and sustains the Buddha-dharmakāya—even up to the body without a basis—through forms that are like illusions, as extensively explained in the sūtras.
Sudhana first beheld the City-Ruling Goddess named Ratnanetra.
That she was "surrounded by a complete retinue" signifies that this is the eye of wisdom within compassion; because she guides and receives sentient beings, he beheld her first.

The scattering of variegated precious flower-petals upon Sudhana signifies the entry into the practice of great compassion; it is not a single kind of practice, but rather the performance of immeasurable and manifold practices, which is why he scatters these flowers of many colors over Sudhana.

Furthermore, he exhorted Sudhana with twenty-eight methods for guarding the city of the mind, intending that he practice great compassion while dwelling within the cycle of birth and death, making it vast and limitless.
Within the activities of birth and death, one does not crave sensory objects, but desires only to accomplish the ten powers of the Tathāgata, as explained at length in the sūtras.
This clarifies that one intends to enter into birth and death to fulfill the practice of great compassion, without abandoning the work of wisdom.
The Dharma of primordial purity and the perfection of great compassion pervade the entire world; it is called "harmony" because it is non-dual, allowing nothing to be obstructed.

These twenty-eight methods for guarding the city of the mind are the union of wisdom and compassion, forming the gate of Samantabhadra’s vast practices for entering birth, ensuring that one is neither stained nor separated [from them].
This is because it is the preliminary skillful means for entering birth-and-death and accomplishing great compassion; therefore, one first beholds the Lord of the City, Jewel-Eye.
It further says: "O Son of the Buddha!..."
If a bodhisattva mahāsattva can cultivate the city of the mind in this way, they will be able to accumulate all wholesome dharmas. Why is this?
Because they eliminate all obstacles.

These are the so-called obstacles to seeing the Buddha, obstacles to hearing the Dharma, obstacles to making offerings to the Tathāgata, obstacles to gathering in all sentient beings, and obstacles to purifying the buddha-fields.

These five kinds of obstacles all arise from a mind that seeks after meritorious and wholesome dharmas and fears the cycle of birth and death; they do not belong to those who have truly entered the effortless, spontaneous great compassion.
Therefore, if you now wish to see such a spiritual friend (kalyāṇamitra) of this stage, you shall see them without effort by constantly eliminating these five obstructive states of mind.

By clarifying the fulfillment of the ten stages of the path and entering the state of Equal Enlightenment, one dwells within the ocean of sentient beings in the world through the great compassion of Samantabhadra; only by removing these five obstacles can one then behold the body of Māyā.

This is to neither seek transcendence from the world, nor seek merit, nor seek to see the Buddha, nor seek to hear the Dharma; rather, it is purely through non-active great compassion to flow along with all sentient beings in the stream of birth and death, teaching and benefiting them, without any seeking for karmic rewards by body or mind, nor any fear of birth and death.

At that time, there was a body-guard deity named Padmadharmaguṇa, surrounded before and behind by immeasurable deities of exquisite flower radiance; emerging from the site of enlightenment, they stayed in mid-air, praising him with various sublime voices.
In this realm of the ocean of birth and death, he dwells in the practice of the emptiness of phenomena, fulfilling it without defilement.

From her ear-ornaments, Lady Māyā emitted nets of light of immeasurable colors, universally illuminating the boundless worlds of all Buddhas, enabling Sudhana to see all the Buddhas in the infinite lands of the ten directions.
That net of light circled the world to the right, returned after one circuit, and entered the crown of Sudhana’s head, pervading even all the pores of his body.
Sudhana immediately attained the eye of pure clarity, because he was forever freed from the darkness of all ignorance;
he attained the unobscured eye, because he was able to comprehend the nature of all sentient beings.
This is explained in detail as stated in the sutras.
Why does the ear ornament emit light?
Because among the six sense faculties, the mental faculty (*manas*) accomplishes the work of wisdom, while among the other five faculties, the ear faculty is preeminent in its function.

This symbolizes great compassion that rescues beings from the ocean of suffering; throughout the entire realm of phenomena (*dharmadhātu*), all sentient beings are saved as soon as they hear the voice, without waiting for the manifestation of the physical body.
Furthermore, it is because the ear is able to hear at a distance, surpassing the other four sense organs.

For instance, when thunder rolls for a hundred *li*, the faculty of hearing perceives it; if there is a great sound, it is heard even at a thousand *li*. The other four faculties cannot reach such a distance.
This illustrates that the light of compassion takes the faculty of hearing as its essence: this light first illuminates the Buddha-lands and subsequently illuminates the world.
With the light of great compassion, he illuminates the Buddha-land and the sentient-being land as one body without duality.

It enters through the crown of Sudhana’s head and subsequently pervades his entire body, entering all the way down to every pore; this clarifies that the light of great compassion universally extends everywhere, entering both the high and the low equally, for their essence is of one single nature.

The light of great wisdom arises from between the eyebrows; the light of receiving birth arises from the navel wheel; the light of great compassion arises from Māyā’s ear-ornament; the light of the forty stages of mind arises from the palms of the hands; the light of the ten levels of faith arises from the thousand-spoked wheels beneath the soles of the feet; the light of the ten abodes arises from the tips of the toes; the light of the ten practices arises from the tops of the ankles; and the light of the ten dedications arises from the knees.

Among the ten stages (*daśabhūmi*), in the sixth stage, the bhikṣu Sāgaramegha emits from his eyes rays of light like solar discs that illuminate the sufferings of the evil realms. When Sudhana receives this light and it enters his body, he is able to comprehend the nature of all sentient beings; this is because, through great compassion of identical essence (*samatā-mahākaruṇā*), he is able to comprehend the nature of all sentient beings.

Next, he saw the rākṣasa king named Sunetra, who guards the Bodhisattva Hall; together with ten thousand rākṣasas as his retinue, he was in the midst of the sky, scattering various exquisite flowers over Sudhana.
It was revealed that this rākṣasī lived within the great ocean; she possessed great power, was able to devour sentient beings at will, and could also travel through the air.

This clarifies that Bodhisattvas, by means of the great wisdom of the emptiness of phenomena, constantly dwell within the ocean of birth and death to protect all sentient beings without ever abandoning them, taking this very state as their palace.
Because he is able to consume the blood, flesh, and the feverish afflictions of ignorance, greed, hatred, delusion, and craving of all sentient beings, he is represented by the King of Rākṣasas.
His dwelling in the great ocean and his capacity for swift, violent destruction serve as his symbolic attributes.
As for the scattering of various flowers upon Sudhana, it is because great compassion is his practice; therefore, he scatters the flowers.
He exhorts and praises Sudhana, causing him to enter the practice of great compassion, as explained at length in the sutra.
The Rākṣasa King spoke to Sudhana regarding the method for seeking spiritual friends: "Noble son!
You should prostrate toward the ten directions and seek spiritual friends."
With right mindfulness, one contemplates all objects of experience while seeking a spiritual friend (*kalyāṇamitra*).
With courageous mastery, one travels throughout the ten directions while seeking a spiritual friend.
Even when observing the body and the mind as being like an illusion, a dream, or a shadow, one seeks a spiritual friend.
Sudhana accepted and practiced these instructions; immediately, he beheld a great jewel lotus springing forth from the earth, with all its adornments as extensively described in the sutra.
Taking great compassion as the ground and the practice of great compassion as the lotus flower,
one who is able to give rise to the mind of great compassion becomes the body of Lady Māyā.

The birth of all Buddhas arises from wisdom through compassion; by means of this wisdom, they realize that all phenomena are produced as illusory manifestations of great wisdom and great compassion, thereby delivering sentient beings.

Within this wisdom that is like an illusion, the illusory manifestations arise with sovereign non-obstruction; yet such mastery is ultimately unattainable, for it is the very function of great wisdom and great compassion.

This wisdom is pure like space; one should abide in the maintenance of emptiness, rather than merely following after compassion in one's conduct. To become deluded regarding the gateway of this wisdom is not permissible; all aspects must be perfectly and fully prepared.
Just as the City-Ruling Goddess once brought together the practice of compassion and wisdom,
so too do the body-attendant spirits and the earrings of Māyā emit light, once again bringing together the essence and function of wisdom and compassion.
The Rākṣasa King once brought together the essence of wisdom and compassion;

thus, after he had exhorted and harmonized them three times and the sequence of causal conditions for the contemplative practice was completed, a lotus flower suddenly sprang forth from the earth, adorned with all manner of jewels, and Māyā sat upon its center.
Seated upon a throne of manifold exquisite jewels, he manifests emanated adornments from within all manner of ornaments.
Together with Lady Māyā, they produce clouds of emanated bodies that pervade the ten directions, bringing all sentient beings to fulfillment, as extensively described in the sutras.
Even up to the point where Sudhana and others, emanated by Māyā, all appeared before her, as described at length in the sutra.

Just as the physical form of Lady Māyā remained as it was originally, she was able to contain within her womb an ocean-like assembly of Bodhisattvas numbering as many as the atoms in ten Buddha-fields, as well as an assembly of eighty thousand nāgas and other beings.

When the Bodhisattva was conceived in the womb, he moved with sovereign ease within the womb of Lady Māyā; in a single step he traversed a trichiliocosm, and every step was likewise so, until he had universally practiced all the deeds of Samantabhadra.

The Universal Worthy Practitioner (Samantabhadra-caryā) encompasses within it the birth and the teaching of sentient beings by all Bodhisattvas; therefore, one should know that this is precisely the embodiment of the great compassionate mother of all Buddhas.
As it is said in the sutra, it cannot be fully described.
When Sudhana asked Māyā about the duration of time since she attained this Dharma, she replied:

"In the remote past, beyond an inconceivable number of kalpas—beyond what can be known by the supernatural powers or the divine eye of bodhisattvas in their final birth—this is the duration of time since I attained this Dharma."
From the passage "I have known only this Bodhisattva’s liberation door of the illusory wisdom of great vows" onwards, this is the advancement through the recommendation of virtues.
Here, the second *pāramitā*, that of morality (*śīla*), is primary, while the remaining nine serve as its companions.
"Good friend!
In this world, among the Trāyastriṃśa gods, there is a king named Samprajanya; he is the very same Samprajanya Devaputra who was previously mentioned among the ten stages."
That king had a daughter named Devendraprabhā (Heavenly Lord Light). She took wisdom as her station and compassion as the essence of her precepts (*śīla*).
Since the Heavenly Lord represents wisdom and the daughter represents compassion, she took the perfection of wisdom and compassion within this station as the essence of her precepts.
Regarding the name "Light of the Lord of Devas": "Deva" signifies purity.
"Lord" refers to entering into the midst of birth and death to uphold and maintain the teachings for the benefit of sentient beings.
"Light" signifies that although one dwells amidst the defilements of birth and death, one acts in concert with great compassion to gather in and sustain sentient beings.
Being untainted by the same fetters and fully endowed with the light of precepts, he is named Lord of Celestial Light (Devendraprabha).
He attains the liberation door of unimpeded mindfulness, pure adornment.
The third perfection, patience (*kṣānti-pāramitā*), is primary, while the remaining nine serve as its companions.
In the city of Kapilavastu, there was a teacher of children named Viśvāmitra.
When Sudhana requested the Dharma from him, he pointed out that within this city there was a child named Śilpabhijña.

These two spiritual friends together form a relationship of principal and attendant; by analogy with the Confucian tradition, they are like Kong Qiu and Yan Hui, for the purpose of instructing the ignorant and young.
One youth recited the forty-two letters of the alphabet, as fully described in the sutra.

When he recited these forty-two letters, he took the forty-two *prajñāpāramitās* as his primary focus, thereby entering immeasurable and innumerable gates of *prajñāpāramitā*; this is the liberation gate of the Bodhisattva Skillfully Knowing All Arts (*Suvikrāntavikrāmi*).
In the fourth [perfection], the perfection of diligence is primary, with the other nine as its companions.
In the fifth, the perfection of meditative concentration is primary, with the other nine as its companions.
In this kingdom of Magadha, there is a village; within it is a city named Vartanī, where there dwells a female lay follower (upāsikā) named Bhadraśrī.
This city is located in South India; it is named Anandavardhana, where one attains the site of enlightenment (bodhimaṇḍa) that is without dependence.
It is taught that within each of the six sense bases, one individually attains the nature of inexhaustible wisdom.

There is nothing among worldly and world-transcending phenomena that he does not fully understand; he is extensively proficient in the principles of yin and yang, the five elements, medical prescriptions, and all arts and crafts, taking their practical application as the essence of dhyāna.
The sixth, the perfection of wisdom (prajñāpāramitā), is the principal, while the other nine are its companions.
To the south there is a city named Kṣetravatī; therein dwells a householder named Dṛḍhavimukti.

Regarding the attainment of the dharma-gate named "The Bodhisattva’s Unattached Mind and Pure Adornment": because the essence of wisdom is fundamentally without attachment and all mental objects are entirely non-existent, it is called "pure. Because wondrous wisdom can generate the roots of goodness in sentient beings, the city is named "Fertile Field. Because wisdom can shatter ignorance, the elder is named "Firm."
The seventh, the perfection of skillful means (*upāya-pāramitā*), is primary, while the other nine serve as its companions.
In this very city there is an elder named *Candraprabha* (Wonderful Moon).

Because the sixth, the perfection of wisdom (*prajñā-pāramitā*), is not distinct from the perfection of skillful means, and because wisdom is able to purify afflictions (*kleśa*), he is named Wonderful Moon.

Although they enter into birth and death through the practice of skillful means, because they are always conjoined with pure wisdom, their abodes are filled with radiance; thus, they attain the Dharma-gate of the Radiance of Wisdom.
The eighth vow takes the perfection (*pāramitā*) as its primary focus, with the remaining nine as its companions.
To the south there is a city named "Birth" (*Utpāda*).
Because the sublime wisdom of non-effortful clarity manifests before one, and because of the practice of great compassion through the power of original vows, the city is named "Birth."
There was an elder named Ajitasena, who, by means of effortless wisdom (*anābhoga-jñāna*), skillfully refuted the heterodox paths such that none could surpass him; thus he was named Ajitasena.

He had attained the Dharma-gate of the Inexhaustible Mark, which, through effortless wisdom, is as vast as space; in all worlds, he constantly manifests infinite physical forms equal in number to sentient beings, never failing to deliver them.
The ninth power, the perfection of power (*bala-pāramitā*), is the principal, with the other nine serving as its companions.

To the south of this city is a village named Dharma; this represents the station of the Dharma-preacher, for all the myriad objects of the world are collectively gathered here as the "Dharma-village."
There was a brahmin named Most Tranquil (Paramaśānta); because he symbolized that the mind and all phenomena are universally tranquil, there was nowhere in any direction that was not tranquil.
Since a brahmin is one who is tranquil, he symbolized that there is no phenomenon in the world that is not tranquil.

Regarding those who attain liberation through speech of sincere vows: because their spoken words emerge with clarity, being truthful and entirely free from falsehood, and because they accord with whatever is sought by the thoughts and vows of sentient beings, it is called "speech of sincere vows."
Furthermore, the words he himself utters are never altered or changed; they are all fit to be the Dharma.
The tenth, the perfection of wisdom (*prajñāpāramitā*), is the sovereign, while the remaining nine serve as its companions.

To the south there is a city named Wondrous Flower Gate (*Citrakusumadvāra*); it signifies that in this stage, wondrous conduct is perfected and the practices of wisdom and compassion are complete, such that one manifests bodies for all sentient beings throughout the ten directions according to their inclinations, pervading them all at once.
The boy named Śrīsaṃbhava symbolizes wisdom;
the girl named Guṇavatī symbolizes compassion.
Since the two practices of wisdom and compassion are already perfected at this stage, they are represented by a single male and female together forming one position.

Furthermore, because they dwell eternally throughout the ten directions and practice all deeds in common with others, they gather in and transform sentient beings according to the flow of conditions to benefit them.
Since their wisdom and compassion are free from the taints of habitual tendencies, they manifest in the forms of boys and girls.
In truth, however, it is essential that young boys and girls be used, for the Buddha’s conduct follows this principle.

Furthermore, to represent how all practitioners of the path must always possess compassion, gentleness, humility, and docility, being free from self-conceit and arrogance, he uses young boys and girls as symbols.

In all lands, they constantly manifest various bodies through the illusion of wisdom, performing various deeds, assuming various forms and appearances, and transforming various sentient beings; without past or present, and without end or beginning, they are ever-present and never cease.

Just as an emanated person is born, and just as an illusory person dwells in the world to transform illusory sentient beings—being ordinary, pervasive, and equal—one thus attains the gate of dwelling like an illusion.
Born through the illusion of wisdom, one dwells in the dharma of illusory dwelling; being without mind, intellect, or consciousness, one transforms and benefits sentient beings.
The following fifty spiritual friends represent the fulfillment of the five stages of practice.

For instance, Maitreya Tathāgata in the land of Sāgara is the fundamental wisdom that encompasses the three periods of time; while residing within the pavilion, he points back to Sudhana to have him see his first spiritual friend, Mañjuśrī, thereby clarifying that the ultimate fruit is not separate from the cause, for time does not shift and wisdom does not differ.

They then hear the name of Samantabhadra Bodhisattva, and even before reaching the Vajragarbha Lotus Throne at the site of enlightenment, they give rise to the aspiration to see their own bodies become equal to the body of Samantabhadra.

Samantabhadra rubbed Sudhana’s crown; this was the fulfillment of a single lifetime of practice, wherein the five stages of cultivation were perfected without departing from the initial arousal of the bodhicitta.

The fundamental, universally radiant, adamantine wisdom—the formless Dharmakāya—brings to completion the boundless, wondrous practices of Samantabhadra. Time does not shift, wisdom does not change, and place does not move; it is like a person in a dream who, without leaving a single location, a single time, a single body, or a single mind, perceives in the dream various years, months, days, and times, travels through various lands, and performs various deeds.
Yet, suddenly awakening, one realizes that this did not depart from the original single moment of dreaming.

By clarifying fundamental wisdom (*mūla-jñāna*), one contemplates all worldly phenomena and realms as being like a dreamer who has awakened: all things neither shift nor move; they are like light and shadow, like illusory beings dwelling in the world—without mind or substance, neither extending nor contracting.
In every place, Mañjuśrī uttered these verses in unison:

"In a single thought-moment, one universally contemplates immeasurable eons; there is no going, no coming, and no abiding. Thus understanding the matters of the three periods of time, one transcends all skillful means and accomplishes the Ten Powers."

By means of Mañjuśrī’s clarity regarding the signless Dharma-body and emptiness-wisdom, the Buddha is the fundamental wisdom of universal radiance, while Samantabhadra is the differentiated wisdom and myriad practices within that fundamental wisdom.
By means of these three dharmas, the gate of the perfection of the essence and function of the single dharma is established.
Within the five stages, the fiftyfold sequence of cause and effect from beginning to end constitutes the gate of the pervasive unity of essence and function.
All take the ten pāramitās as the essential substance of their practice; within each one, the ten are complete, and within the ten, the hundred are complete.
Within the five stages, according to the different points of advancement, there are five hundred pāramitās within these five stages.

Within the five stages, there are fifty spiritual friends (*kalyāṇamitra*), each of whom possesses both cause and fruit; thus, the fifty layers of cause and fruit together constitute one hundred. These do not depart from the fundamental ten *pāramitās*, which serve as the tenfold basis. In total, there are one hundred and ten layers of cause and fruit, all of which take the ten *pāramitās* as the essential substance of their practice.

Taking the fundamental wisdom of Mañjuśrī and the Buddha, and the differentiated wisdom of Samantabhadra, as its great essence, one should practice by emulating them; thus, one will not lose the Great Way, will forever sever the net of doubt, and will not err in one's cultivation.
It is like a great highway where signboards are well-placed to enable travelers to eliminate their doubts.
Within this stage of Bodhi, the stage of Samantabhadra’s practice does not manifest entirely distinct signs from those of worldly people, so as to attract the common masses.

After attaining the Way, one constantly dwells within the birth-and-death of the ten directions, manifesting bodies through the illusion of wisdom according to the different perceptions of sentient beings, thereby perpetually transforming and benefiting them.
They abide in the gate of illusory dwelling, for there is neither emergence nor disappearance.
Because their wondrous function of spiritual wisdom is all-pervasive, it is eternally without activity.
Because their wisdom is like an echo that produces sound in response to objects, it is without arising, abiding, or ceasing.
By means of the sun of the wisdom that is like space, one constantly and universally illumines the ten directions with great radiance, for there is neither center nor periphery.
By means of the realm of wisdom, one enters the body of ten light-reflection bodies, which, like the net of Indra, consist of layered images, for they neither go nor come.

Just as the youth Guṇākara and the maiden Guṇavatī, with wisdom and compassion equally perfected, abide within the gate of illusory dwelling; through the illusory power of their wisdom, they manifest bodies commensurate with those of all sentient beings throughout the ten directions, teaching and bringing all beings to fulfillment upon the path of Samantabhadra, without ever ceasing.

A Brief Explanation of the Stages of Practice in the New Avataṃsaka Sūtra: Resolving Doubts, Volume IV, Part II. Postscript to the *Treatise on Resolving Doubts*. Composed by the Elder Li of Fángshān, Shòuyáng County, Tàiyuán Prefecture. Recorded at Zhāohuà Temple.
In the seventh month of the Wushen year of the Yuanyou era, Shangying traveled to Mount Wutai; at midnight, amidst a golden light at Bimoyan, he beheld Mañjuśrī Bodhisattva.
Moved by a profound realization regarding the passage of time, he vowed to exhaustively study the Buddha’s teachings.

Retiring to his quarters, he examined the *Huayan jing yishu* (Commentary on the Meaning of the Avatamsaka Sutra), yet found it so vast and diffuse that he could discern no underlying order or system.

In the ninth month, while traveling on inspection to Shouyang, he heard that thirty-five li to the east of the county lay Fangshan Zhaohua Monastery, the very site where the Elder [Nāgārjuna] composed his treatises; thereupon, having purified himself through fasting and ritual observance, he went to pay his respects.

Upon arriving, beneath a ruined house and amidst a scattered collection of scrolls, he found the *Huayan Xingxiu Jueyi Lun* (Treatise on Resolving Doubts Concerning the Practice of Avataṃsaka) in four fascicles; after reading several sheets with haste, his doubts were suddenly dispelled.
He questioned the presiding monk, saying, "This is a place where sages and worthies have dwelt; why is it so dilapidated?
The monk replied:
"The elder has been sitting in death on this mountain for a long time.
Wherever his spirit roams and wherever his karmic conditions lead, the years and harvests are always abundant and things suffer no blight or pestilence."

"The people of this region have been consorting with the ghosts of Mount Fang, treating them as if they were their elders; they lack reverence for my elders, and thus our temple has fallen into poverty.

I, following the example of the envoys of antiquity who destroyed licentious sacrifices—often numbering in the thousands—immediately moved the county authorities to abolish the shrines of the ghosts, installed the images of the elders, and prayed for blessings upon the people.

On the seventh day of the tenth month, the foundation was laid; on the eighth day, a white circular light appeared to the south of the mountain, whereupon the elders bowed their heads and wept with grief, saying:
"We did not know that the merit of the Elder would extend to our land."
"I request that you renovate the monastery together.
As his mind opened to the task, it was as if clouds arose; he responded in harmony without being prompted.
When the head monk sent Yuanlai to inform him, the Grand Master Zeng Gongzi Xuan heard of the matter and said to Shangying:

"Son, why do you not clarify the Elder’s intention and record it, so that those who study the *Avataṃsaka* may further develop great faith and know what to revere? In this way, the Elder’s emission of light to entrust this task to you will not have been in vain."
Shangying said: "How could someone as ignorant and obstructed as I be worthy of knowing the Venerable One?
Nevertheless, allow me to attempt to peer at it through the tube."
Now, as for the teaching of the *Avataṃsaka*, it concerns the Buddha and the matters of the Bodhisattvas of the One Vehicle!

From beginning to end, it is a single thought-moment; past and present are one time; cause and effect are one Buddha; ordinary beings and sages are one nature; the ten directions are one land; the three realms are one essence; the periods of the True, Semblance, and Final Dharma are one teaching; and the beginning, middle, and end are one limit.
It manifests directly at that very place, without involving emotional attachments or intellectual interpretations.
Taking the ten levels of faith as the beginning of entering the Buddha-way and taking the ten stages (bhūmis) as the end of attaining Buddhahood,
the ten abidings, ten practices, ten transferences, ten stages, and the eleventh stage are termed the five positions.
Regarding "the six stages possessing ten": this means that the ten *pāramitās* serve as the primary factors.
In each of the five preceding stages, there are fifty causes and fifty fruits; adding the five causes and five fruits of the fundamental stage itself results in one hundred and ten.
This is how the Buddha-field of the Avataṃsaka world and the Dharma-gate of the youth Sudhana were accomplished.
Why is there one added to the one hundred and ten worlds of the Avataṃsaka?
First is the stage of the Buddha, which is the cause of all dharmas.
The five stages are the dharmas that are indicated.
Sudhana is the person who inquires into the Dharma and puts it into practice.
Regarding the "fifty-three supreme friends": the fifty refer to the five stages (*pañcāvasthā*), while the three refer to Mañjuśrī, Samantabhadra, and Maitreya.

This scripture takes Vairocana as the essence of fundamental wisdom (*mūlaprajñā*), Mañjuśrī as wondrous wisdom (*prajñā*), and Samantabhadra as the myriad practices (*sarvacaryā*); it is precisely through these that one gives rise to faith and enters the five stages.

Thus, when wisdom is the essence and practice is its function, and that practice reaches perfection such that one enters the Dharma-realm, then practice becomes the essence and wisdom becomes its function.

When essence and function mutually interpenetrate and principle and phenomena thoroughly permeate one another, there is neither dependence nor cultivation, and the fruit of Buddhahood is realized; therefore, this is attributed to the future Buddha Maitreya.
Those in the Ten Faiths who take form as their realm have not yet transcended the dust of form.
Those in the Ten Abidings who take the flower as their realm signify the blossoming of principle and phenomena.
Those in the Ten Practices who take wisdom as their realm signify the perfect clarity of concentration and wisdom.
Regarding the tenth dedication, "taking the wondrous as the land," this refers to the sovereign mastery of wondrous function.
The various names and titles are alternative designations for the essence of wisdom; by contemplating these names, one comes to know the practices that have been cultivated.
The various adornments are the fruits resulting from the reliance upon one's nature and conduct; by observing these fruits, one knows the causes of the practices that produced them.

Great compassion that extensively saves is called the ocean; that which removes heat and brings coolness is called the moon; that which universally rains down the rain of Dharma is called the cloud; and that which encompasses all phenomena is called the treasury.
Adorning their foremost leaders, they are called Ratnaśikhin (Jewel-Crested).
Being simultaneous in cause and effect, dwelling in the world without being defiled, they are called Padma (Lotus).
Subduing false views while remaining upright and immovable, they are called Dhvaja (Banner).
The middle way of compassion and wisdom is called *zhāi* (fasting); the universal permeation of one's nature and vows is called *xiāng* (incense).
That which is accomplished without action is Heaven;
that which responds without fixed direction is the Spirit (*shén*).
That which is great without being external is the King.
That which flies and hides while bringing rain is the Dragon.
That which dwells in the sea of birth and death without sinking is the Asura.
Those who grasp the roots [of practice], mature sentient beings, and reach the shore of Buddhahood are the garuḍas.
Those who are neither ordinary nor holy, and whose nature remains doubtful and unknowable, are the kiṃnaras.
Those that move on their chests, crawling along with humility and grace to benefit all beings, are *mahoragas*.
Those who provide protection and vigilance are *yakṣas*.
Those who share the same miserable realms as others yet extinguish their poverty and suffering are *kumbhāṇḍas*.
Those who delight in the sound of the Dharma are the gandharvas. Gold is firm, hard, yellow, and white.
The wheel is circular and complete.
Crystal is for its translucent brilliance; lapis lazuli is for its luminosity.
That which is pure and stainless is called *maṇi*; that which filters and rescues those submerged is called a net.
That which is lofty, prominent, and preeminent is called a stem or trunk; that which unfolds and provides shelter is called a flower or leaf.
Nurturing and benefiting sentient beings is called the palace; the faculty of contemplative observation is called the pavilion.
Fearlessness is called the lion; transcending the mundane dust is called the terrace and the belvedere.
Leaving the secular world, one is called a bhikṣu; entering the marketplace, one is called a lay practitioner or a householder. Being similar to non-Buddhists, one is called a rishi or a brāhmaṇa.
Being compassionate yet unstained, one is called a woman; giving rise to wisdom through compassion, one is called a mother.
These phenomena of the *Avataṃsaka* represent the great purport of the Dharma.

As for how a single word contains ten thousand dharmas and pervades all things—its vastness and profundity are such that who other than the Elder [Fazang] could discern its teachings and unravel its subtleties?
The elder’s name was Tongxuan; some called him the Son of the Tang Dynasty, while others said he was a native of Cangzhou, though none can provide detailed accounts.
He was likely a manifested being of Mañjuśrī and Samantabhadra.
In the seventh year of the Kaiyuan era, he went into seclusion at a clay grotto on Mount Fang to compose his treatise.
He passed away on the twenty-eighth day of the third month in the eighteenth year; he was buried with a stone cairn to the north of the mountain.
During the Qingtai era, villagers cleared away stones and discovered a series of golden skeletal remains that were linked like beads; when struck, they produced a sound like reed pipes.
In the third year of the Tianfu era, a stone pagoda was rebuilt and the relics were interred seven *li* to the east of the mountain, which is currently located within the borders of Meng County.

The narrator says that [the Master] subdued tigers to carry his scriptures and transformed divine dragons into springs; by day, celestial maidens attended him, and by night, the light from his teeth served as lamps.

On the day he manifested parinirvāṇa, birds and beasts wailed in grief and white vapors pierced the heavens. These were all the residual activities of a sage and the natural principles of spiritual resonance.
What the tradition calls "cultivating the mother to reach the child" is close to the truth.
For now, I have omitted all such details and shall not record them here.
